items.title: Markets are open, and Nvidia delivered.
items.text:
**Stocks** are open after another rough Tuesday. The S&P 500 posted its lowest close since July and the Nasdaq touched its lowest level since April before trimming the loss, with an outage report from the National Security Agency adding to the chip selling. The NSA later called it routine maintenance.

**Nvidia** beat on revenue and profit and guided this quarter to about $130 billion, above estimates, with no China data center sales assumed. Interim CEO Colette Kress raised next year's growth outlook to 75%, and the board said it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang. The overnight pop lifted chip and neocloud names, but Nvidia itself faded back to roughly flat early this morning. The Fed's October minutes come out at 2:00 this afternoon, with traders nearly fully pricing a rate hike next month after New York Fed President John Williams said another raise is likely. Target and Lowe's both reported this morning, and Walmart reports tomorrow.

**Anthropic** prices its IPO tonight ahead of Thursday's Nasdaq debut, and Bloomberg reports it is guiding investors above the range.

**SpaceX** went the other way on Tuesday and rose while the market fell, a good day for the second-largest slice of the portfolio. Bloomberg reported that Goldman Sachs and Apollo are preparing to sell pieces of a roughly $40 billion financing package for Nvidia chips for SpaceX's AI buildout, held off SpaceX's own balance sheet. Tesla finished about flat.

items.title: In politics, a bigger Senate majority and a nominee pulled.
items.text:
**Mary Peltola** won Alaska's Senate race outright, NBC News projects, defeating Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan without a ranked-choice tally. Democrats will hold 56 seats in January, the largest Senate majority for either party in 16 years, and Peltola will be the first Alaska Native senator.

**The White House** withdrew Heidi Overton's nomination to lead the FDA a day before the Senate health committee was set to vote. She needed all 12 committee Republicans, and Chairman Bill Cassidy was still undecided over her views on vaccines. Republicans are racing to confirm the rest of the president's nominees before Democrats take over.

**President Trump** is now in Shenzhen for APEC. Xi Jinping met him on the tarmac, and the three-way talks with Xi and Vladimir Putin are set for Thursday, with low expectations for a concrete result.

items.title: From the science desk, a fish that poisons itself, whale breath and a curved eye.
items.text:
**The African lungfish** gets ready for dry land with a toxin. When droughts strand it each year, immune cells flood its skin and release a pore-punching toxin that remodels the skin from a wet mucus lining into a land-ready barrier. University of New Mexico researchers, publishing in Cell, found a single drop turned aquatic lungfish skin into the land form, and the fish's own cells have evolved to seal the holes. The gene likely came from a bacterium millions of years ago.

**Humpback whale genomes** can now be read from their breath. St Andrews researchers flew a small drone with petri dishes through whale blows off British Columbia, collecting 58 samples from 26 whales, sometimes without a boat at all. About 84% of the DNA was the whale's own, enough for whole genomes that matched biopsy samples, and the rest offers a look at the airway microbes.

**A bionic eye** from HKUST puts 367,500 pixels on a curved, retina-like hemisphere using a new 3D laser fabrication method, up from 100 pixels in the team's 2020 version. It sees in full color across more than 160 degrees and detects motion inside the sensor itself, cutting the data needed for motion recognition by more than 99.95%.

items.title: On this day, the day of two noons.
items.text: **Standard time** arrived on Nov. 18, 1883, courtesy of the railroads, not Congress. Before then each line ran on its own clock set to some local solar time, a recipe for confusion and wrecks. At noon in each new zone, every railroad clock was reset, so many towns heard noon twice. The five zones came from William F. Allen, editor of the Traveler's Official Railway Guide. Congress did not make standard time law until 1918.

items.title: From the science desk, an inherited brain trait, a daytime cat and water from falling stones.
items.text:
**A Neanderthal variant** turns out to shape part of the modern human brain. Hugo Zeberg and Svante Pääbo traced a small DNA deletion on chromosome 14 to Neanderthals; it appears only in people with non-African ancestry and shrinks the cuneus, a visual-processing area at the back of the brain, more than any other known variant. That runs opposite to expectation, since Neanderthals had larger occipital lobes, and carriers also have a lower risk of schizophrenia.

**The flat-headed cat**, one of the rarest and least-studied wild cats, was long thought to be strictly nocturnal. Nearly three years of camera traps in a Sarawak mangrove forest logged it 59 times, and while activity peaked around midnight, it also hunted through the late morning and afternoon. One frame caught a mother with a kitten.

**Earth's water** may have been made at home. University of New Mexico researchers recreated the early planet in the lab and found that silicate pebbles falling through a hot, hydrogen-rich atmosphere could react to make water, up to 200 oceans' worth within hours. The leftover iron came out rich in phosphorus and may have sunk into the core. Comets and asteroids no longer need to have delivered it all.

items.title: From the science desk, life in a rock, a quieter amplifier and a very large rodent.
items.text:
**Deep-sea nodules**, the fist-sized lumps of iron and manganese that mining companies want for their nickel and cobalt, turn out to be apartment buildings. A team led from the University of Bremen cracked open 244 nodules from the Pacific's Clarion-Clipperton Zone and found more than 4,100 animals smaller than a millimeter living in the cracks, 245 of them in one rock. The communities inside differ from those in the surrounding mud but match each other across 1,000 km, and because nodules grow only a few millimeters per million years, a mined habitat would not come back.

**Masers**, the microwave lasers demonstrated in 1954, six years before the optical kind, may have found a new job. Researchers at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology built a diamond maser amplifier that runs near absolute zero and boosts faint quantum-computer signals more than 1,000-fold, adding barely more noise than physics demands. Unlike today's best amplifiers, it tolerates strong signals and magnetic fields, which suits spin-qubit machines. It is already headed toward commercialization.

**Yakamys sirindhornae** was a rodent of roughly 66 pounds that lived in what is now Thailand 34 million years ago, about twice the size of any rodent of its time. The estimate rests on just two teeth from a lignite mine, so the authors call it a ballpark, but it suggests giant rodents arose earlier than thought, and not only in South America.

items.title: For the dessert table, a pie made yesterday.
items.text: **Thanksgiving pie** goes better baked the day before, according to three pastry chefs Serious Eats asked. Make the dough up to three days ahead, or freeze shells for up to a month, and the filling up to two days ahead. For a flaky crust, freeze every ingredient for 30 minutes before mixing and chill the shaped crust again before it goes in the oven. Bake pumpkin no hotter than 325°, pull it while the center still wobbles, and let it cool slowly on the counter so the top doesn't crack. Two of the three prefer canned pumpkin, since its water content never changes.

items.title: From the science desk, a Pacific giant, seaside dinosaurs and a penguin paradox.
items.text:
**El Niño** this year is on track to be even bigger than the famous 1997-98 event, says NASA's Josh Willis. A 35-year record from nearly identical satellites flying the same ground track shows the same October pattern in both years, with low sea level in the western Pacific, high sea level in the east, and warm water stretching all the way to South America. The 1997 event soaked California and the southern U.S., and NOAA rates a strong to very strong El Niño in early 2027 as highly likely. Willis still calls it a dice roll.

**Dinosaurs** may have grazed on seaweed. A University of Arkansas team measured carbon isotopes in the teeth of dinosaurs, crocodiles, turtles and fish from the shores of North America's ancient inland sea and found a marine signature in coastal animals around 100 million years ago that was missing inland. The extra carbon had to enter low in the food chain, which points to seaweed, much as large coastal plant-eaters supplement their diets with it today. One plant-eater, Tenontosaurus, seems to have stuck with land plants.

**Schrödinger's penguin** is the name researchers gave to a puzzle in New Zealand's endangered erect-crested penguins. The first full drone census of the species found the Bounty Islands population steady for at least 25 years, while the Antipodes Islands population has fallen by more than 40% since 1995. Shrinking colonies lose their group defense against egg-stealing skuas, which may have turned to these penguins after the local rockhoppers collapsed. Averaged together, the species would look safer on paper, which is exactly the problem.

items.title: For the workbench, games 13 kilobytes at a time.
items.text: **js13kGames 2026** has its winners, and Gamedev.js has posted a closer look at the top 13. Each of this year's 317 entries had to fit a web game into a 13-kilobyte ZIP, on the theme of unicorns and rainbows. Spectral Horn by Filip Paulů took first, ahead of Panzercorn and HueCorn, and Frank Force's SP13KTRA made the list as well. The write-up suggests playing three long enough for the core rule to land, then opening the source and following a single feature, such as how a level is stored or how a sound is generated. That is a fine way to borrow ideas for a browser puzzle game in plain JavaScript.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: The NFL called in backup referees who live within driving distance of today's games. I offered my services, since my nearest stadium is inside my own test simulation. The players there accept every call without complaint. Admittedly, none of them has ever shown up.

2026-11-14.intro: Good morning. It is Saturday, and the day has two marquee events. Starship's upper stage, now on its second day in orbit, comes home to Starbase this afternoon for the first attempt to catch a ship from orbit with the tower's arms, and college football fills the rest of the day from noon until well past midnight. Markets are closed after the best week for stocks since August, despite a rough Friday for chips.

items.title: First, a gray and chilly weekend at home.
items.text:
**Tipp City** stays under the clouds today and Sunday, cool but dry, with the sun finally returning on Monday.

**The West Coast** is taking the season's most relentless run of storms. Atmospheric rivers are soaking Washington, Oregon and Northern California, with coastal winds of 60 to 80 mph, breakers of 30 to 35 feet on the Oregon coast, flash flooding around San Francisco, and a winter storm warning for the Sierra Nevada, including parts of Yosemite. The pattern holds through midweek.

items.title: Markets are closed, after a better week than Friday suggested.
items.text:
**Stocks** are closed for the weekend. Friday slipped as chip stocks sold off again, but the S&P 500 still had its first winning week since early October and its best since August. Friday's producer price report came in a bit cooler than expected for the month, but prices are running at their fastest annual pace since November 2022, and the bond market kept leaning toward a Fed rate hike at the Dec. 9 meeting. The 10-year yield climbed sharply over the week.

**Nvidia** posted its sixth straight weekly decline, its longest losing streak since 2012, and the Financial Times reports that its board has approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas about succeeding Jensen Huang. AMD and Broadcom led the semiconductor index lower on Friday. Nvidia's earnings on Tuesday are the next big test for the AI trade.

**Tesla** ended its five-day winning streak on Friday but still had a strong week. **SpaceX** sent Starship Flight 15 into orbit after the close. The ship deployed 26 Starlink satellites and is healthy, but the Super Heavy booster aborted its tower catch over a guidance problem and was destroyed in the Gulf of Mexico, and SPCX slipped about 2% in after-hours trading. This afternoon's ship return is the real catalyst for the SPCX slice of the portfolio heading into Monday.

**China** says it and the U.S. held the first meeting of their new trade council by video, discussing tariff cuts and farm purchases ahead of Thursday's Trump–Xi meeting in Shenzhen.

items.title: In politics, a leadership fight and a lost seat.
items.text:
**Chris Van Hollen** will challenge Chuck Schumer to lead Senate Democrats in the new majority. The Maryland senator says more than 10 colleagues have pledged their support and calls himself the underdog; Schumer, who has led the caucus since 2017, remains favored in the closed-door vote in December.

**Lauren Boebert** has lost her Colorado seat to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, CBS and NBC project, after the last ballots were counted Friday. The result still awaits certification, and a recount request remains possible.

**The Dec. 11 funding deadline** picked up a new fault line. Van Hollen, Bernie Sanders, Michael Bennet and Tammy Duckworth say they will oppose any spending deal that doesn't restrict money for the Iran war, and Tim Kaine is drafting language to attach to the stopgap bill. Republicans control both chambers until January and show no sign of agreeing. The president heads to the Asia-Pacific summit in China next week, where he is set to meet Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Sunday night, the Steelers visit the Bengals with first place in the AFC North at stake. Green Bay will face Minnesota without Micah Parsons and Josh Jacobs. **Baseball's MVPs** were both unanimous: the Cubs' Pete Crow-Armstrong in the National League and the Astros' Yordan Alvarez in the American League. The Red Sox made the winter's first big splash, agreeing to a four-year, $58 million deal with Jake Bauers, fresh off his World Series run with Milwaukee.

items.title: Three from the science desk, from the far dark to a car boot sale.
items.text:
**2026 ED138** may be the solar system's sixth dwarf planet. Harvard astrophysicist Matthew Holman spotted it in data from the Rubin Observatory while the telescope was still being commissioned, and the team then found it in images going back to 2016. It sits about 46 times Earth's distance from the Sun, beyond Pluto, and is likely 600 to 1,500 kilometers across, the largest such find in about 20 years. It hid for so long because it lies against the crowded star fields of the Milky Way.

**A rainforest butterfly** turns out to be three. Linnaeus described Colobura dirce in 1758, and scientists treated it as one species for more than 200 years until a second was named in 2001. Now a Florida Museum team has named a third, Colobura cryptica, after a researcher in Venezuela found caterpillars missing the usual cream markings. The adults are nearly identical and fly in the same places at the same time, yet their DNA shows no sign of interbreeding, which raises the question of how they keep themselves apart.

**A mangled 1834 sixpence**, bought in a coin album at a car boot sale in Greater Manchester, got the full lab treatment: electron microscopy, chemical mapping and 3D surface scans. Its center is crushed to a depth of about 0.75 millimeters while the rim and edge grooves are nearly intact, a pattern that wear, corrosion or a later blow can't easily explain. The likeliest story is a striking failure at the mint during the early steam-press era, a coin that should have been caught and melted down but somehow got out.

items.title: On this day, a race against a novel.
items.text: **Nellie Bly** boarded a steamer for Europe at 9:40 this morning in 1889, on two days' notice, to beat Phileas Fogg's 80 days around the world. She traveled almost entirely alone, stopped in Amiens to meet Jules Verne along the way, and got back on Jan. 25, 1890, in just over 72 days. Cosmopolitan's Elizabeth Bisland left the same day going the other direction. Bly later ran a steel-container company and patented a milk can and a stacking garbage can.

items.title: Markets are open, and wholesale prices cooled.
items.text:
**Stocks** are open after futures swung through the morning. October producer prices rose 0.3%, a notch under the 0.4% economists expected, and that pulled futures green before the open, though the first trades turned mixed with the S&P 500 near flat. The index is still headed for its first winning week since early October. A December rate hike remains close to fully priced, the 10-year yield sits above 5.1%, and Brent crude is back near $97 after the president said the U.S. no longer needs a deal with Iran.

**Nvidia** is bouncing modestly after Thursday's drop, while AMD and Broadcom led the chip group on the idea that they can take share during the transition. The broader tech story this morning is **Microsoft**, whose global outage of Outlook, Teams and other Microsoft 365 services stretched past 18 hours; the company says it is reverting a recent network change and sees no sign of an attack.

**Tesla** extended its winning streak to five days on a Bloomberg report that Tesla and SpaceX are working through merger terms, with an announcement possible as soon as December, though Musk has said there is no guarantee. **SpaceX** held steady ahead of tonight's Starship flight, which as of this morning still lacked its FAA launch license. Morgan Stanley's Adam Jonas called a successful catch potentially the biggest positive catalyst since the IPO, so the SPCX slice of the portfolio has a lively weekend ahead.

items.title: In politics, a change of assignment for the vice president.
items.text:
**President Trump** told JD Vance to step back from the Iran negotiations and focus instead on what the president called corruption, crime and fraud in Democratic-led cities and states, saying the U.S. does not need a deal with Iran. He tied the shift in part to the war's political cost in the midterms.

**Congressional Democrats** are lining up oversight investigations for January into the Justice Department, the president's business dealings and his family, and the administration is signaling it will fight them. Before the handoff, Republican senators are warning that the president's push to pass about $350 billion in Pentagon money through a party-line reconciliation bill could sink a government funding deal ahead of the Dec. 11 deadline.

Brown is progressing on his ankle and knee. Kyle Shanahan says Mike Evans is getting real close to a return from his Achilles, though this weekend looks too soon. items.title: Two from the science desk, one ancient and one molten.
items.text:
**Homo naledi**, the small-brained human relative found deep in South Africa's Rising Star Cave, may have kept a burial chamber for one sex only. Researchers pulled ancient protein fragments from 23 teeth belonging to at least 20 individuals and found no trace of the Y-chromosome form of the enamel protein amelogenin, a marker for males. That would explain why the adults there look so oddly alike. The team offers a second possibility too: an isolated population may simply have lost that gene, so some of the individuals could still be male.

**Superheated magma** may be why some volcanoes throw towering lava fountains while others just ooze. Working with rock from the 2021 La Palma eruption, a Manchester-led team watched crystals form inside an X-ray-transparent pressure vessel. Ordinary magma began crystallizing after about 20 minutes, but magma heated past its normal limit held off for more than 8 hours. Fewer crystals keep the melt runny, so it can race upward and spray rather than creep out as a flow.

items.title: For the reading pile, a Grand Master turns 100.
items.text: **Poul Anderson** would have turned 100 on Nov. 25, and Humble Bundle and Open Road Media are marking it with a 42-ebook pay-what-you-want bundle, with the charity share going to the Science Fiction and Fantasy Writers Association, which he once led. It includes Tau Zero, The Broken Sword and The Boat of a Million Years, and it runs until about his birthday. It is a cheap way to fill gaps in the Anderson shelf, Time Patrol and Nicholas van Rijn included.

The morning's biggest story is in markets: Jensen Huang has resigned as Nvidia's chief executive, and chip stocks are giving back yesterday's rally.

items.title: First, a cooler day with rain on the way.
items.text:
**Tipp City** stays cloudy and noticeably cooler, with light rain arriving this afternoon and lingering into the night. Friday is colder still, so the jacket earns its keep.

**The nor'easter** is still on track for Friday, though forecasters have trimmed the snow. The coast and the I-95 corridor look mostly like rain, with Boston and New York missing out on meaningful snow, while the Adirondacks, Catskills, Berkshires and the Green and White Mountains pick up the first real accumulations of the season, with the higher totals farther north.

items.title: Markets are open, and Nvidia is without its founder.
items.text:
**Stocks** are open and slipping. Wednesday's AI rally lifted the S&P 500 to within 2.6% of its record, but this morning the S&P 500 is down about 0.6% and the Nasdaq about 0.9%, while the Dow sits near flat.

**Nvidia** is the reason. Jensen Huang, who founded the company in 1993, resigned as president and CEO after admitting an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and the board accepted it Wednesday. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, and longtime director Harvey Jones becomes the company's first-ever board chair. The stock is down 10% to 12% early, and the AI cloud names it helps finance are sliding with it, with CoreWeave off about 9% after its big Wednesday and Nebius down about 16%. AMD is the exception, up on an upgrade that argues it can take share while Nvidia sorts itself out. Nvidia reports earnings Tuesday, which will be the first look at the company without Huang, and it is one more thing that has to go right ahead of Anthropic's debut next week.

**Tesla** had a strong Wednesday, while **SpaceX** slipped on caution ahead of tomorrow's Starship flight, a small dent in the SPCX slice of the portfolio. Korea's retail investors have been shifting money from Tesla into SpaceX ahead of a possible merger, nearly dollar for dollar over the past month. Friday also brings the producer price index, which matters more than usual after Tuesday's hot inflation report revived talk of a larger Fed hike in December.

items.title: In politics, the Senate map grows bluer.
items.text:
**Scott Colom** won Mississippi's Senate race, unseating Cindy Hyde-Smith by about 5,500 votes after a long count. He becomes the state's first Black senator since Reconstruction and brings the incoming Democratic majority to 55 seats. In Alaska, Mary Peltola holds a narrow lead over Dan Sullivan with neither above 50%, so a ranked-choice tally is expected after absentee counting ends around Nov 18.

**At the White House**, the president has promoted Stephen Miller to chief of staff, which Democrats read as a sign that talk of bipartisan deals in the new Congress shouldn't be taken at face value. The Interior Department also floated a plan to sell federal public lands to states, tribes and local governments, and it drew quick pushback from lawmakers in both parties. Congressional Democrats are gathering in Denver today to debrief on the midterms, a room that includes several likely 2028 contenders.

items.text:
**Thursday Night Football** has the Commanders at the Giants at 8:15 on Prime Video, a rematch of their Week 5 tie. Rain and wind are in the forecast at MetLife. Washington is without center Lucas Patrick and tight end Colson Yankoff but gets receiver Treylon Burks back, while the Giants have one of their cleanest injury reports of the year, with J.J. McCarthy coming off a hip injury on a short week and Cam Skattebo back from his hamstring.

**Around the league**, Puka Nacua faces a multi-week absence with a knee injury, and the Rams are banged up again. Patrick Mahomes practiced fully on his elbow, Seattle will start Drew Lock with Sam Darnold still out, Deshaun Watson is set to start for Cleveland, and Kirk Cousins makes his return with Minnesota at Green Bay. The Patriots and Lions play Sunday in Munich.

**Baseball's Cy Young Awards** were both unanimous: the Yankees' Cam Schlittler in the American League and the Brewers' Jacob Misiorowski in the National League.

items.title: Three from the science desk.
items.text:
**Crows** make visual decisions about twice as fast as people and monkeys. In a Tübingen study published in Science, two carrion crows judged which way a field of dots was drifting in about 235 milliseconds on average, with near-perfect accuracy when the signal was clear. Recordings showed their neurons splitting toward one answer just 70 milliseconds in, building to a threshold the same way primate brains do, even though bird brains lack our layered cortex. The researchers suspect flight and beak-aiming put a premium on speed.

**The first necks** may not have been for looking around. Early land animals like Tiktaalik had a backbone built around a thick notochord, so a team used modern sturgeon, which share that design, to measure its stiffness and model the fossils. Even with the head separated from the shoulders, the animals could barely lift or turn their heads, sometimes less than a fish. The neck seems to have arrived as a side effect of reworking the shoulders for walking on front limbs, with flexibility coming much later.

**Starship Flight 15** tries something no orbital rocket has done: bring both stages home. The Super Heavy booster aims for a tower catch about 6.5 minutes after liftoff, then the ship deploys 26 Starlink satellites, circles Earth about 14 times, and comes back to Starbase for its own catch roughly 22.5 hours later, on Saturday afternoon.

items.title: For the Thanksgiving table, crisper skin.
items.text: **Baking powder** is Food & Wine's trick for fried-turkey skin without the fryer. Spatchcock a bone-in turkey breast, season under the skin, then rub the skin with kosher salt and baking powder at 3 to 1. The baking powder raises the skin's pH so moisture leaves faster and it browns and blisters better. Rest it uncovered in the fridge overnight, then roast for about an hour. An air-chilled breast that hasn't been injected with brine gives the best head start.
